1	# Checks — deterministic enforcement of the corpus (design)
2	
3	> **Status: implemented** (issue #127, #131). The runner, the baseline + technology packs, Stop
4	> hook, PreToolUse guard, and the pack-prose loader are live; the corpus is reorganized into
5	> `packs/` (prose + checks, active by declaration) and `skills/` (activity-scoped procedures).
6	> This doc is the rationale and the ongoing design record. The per-rule audit lives in
7	> [docs/conversion-inventory.md](../../docs/conversion-inventory.md).
8	
9	## The problem
10	
11	The corpus enforces style/practice rules as instructions. Instructions have three standing costs:
12	
13	1. **Context** — the always-on baseline loads every session whether or not it's needed, and
14	   adherence degrades as loaded context grows.
15	2. **Silent trigger failure** — soft-loaded docs depend on the agent following their trigger
16	   ("read filePlacement.md before placing a file"), which is itself instruction-following that
17	   fails silently. A rule the agent didn't read can't help.
18	3. **Invisible obsolescence** — a rule a newer Claude Code follows by default keeps costing
19	   tokens and attention forever; nothing measures that it stopped earning its place.
20	
21	A deterministic check inverts all three: it costs zero context until violated, fires whether or
22	not anything was read, and its firing history is measurable — a check that never fails is
23	evidence its rule can retire.
24	
25	## Why this is the right mechanism
26	
27	Anthropic's published guidance says this directly: hooks exist to provide "deterministic control
28	… ensuring certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them"
29	(hooks guide); CLAUDE.md is "context, not enforced" (memory doc); and the core best-practice is
30	"give Claude a check it can run … Claude does the work, runs the check, reads the result, and
31	iterates until the check passes" (best practices). The corpus already states the principle in
32	an agent-practices skill: *"Prose is a request; the
33	post-hoc diff check is the guarantee."* This design scales that sentence up.
34	
35	## What converts — and what doesn't
36	
37	An instruction leaves context only when a deterministic mechanism can carry it. Four targets,
38	picked per rule:
39	
40	| Mechanism | Fits when | Examples from the corpus |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| **Post-hoc check** (this system) | The rule constrains the *state of the repo* after work | file placement, dangling references, workflow lint, lifecycle compliance |
43	| **PreToolUse hook** | The action must be blocked *before* it runs | never delete a remote branch; don't `issue_write`-overwrite an issue body |
44	| **Skill / script** | A *procedure* or *knowledge* with a nameable (or path-scoped) trigger | the merge recipe; the lessons pass; the technology gotcha files |
45	| **Platform setting** | The platform enforces it outright, for free | squash-only merges; branch protection |
46	
47	Two classes deliberately **stay as instructions**:
48	
49	- **Process/judgment rules** — problem-first consensus, bug investigation method, naming
50	  quality. They shape work *in flight* and leave no artifact a check can inspect. Converting
51	  them post-hoc would also catch violations only after the expensive rework they exist to
52	  prevent.
53	- **Platform-gotcha knowledge** (`technologies/`) — split **per gotcha**, by whether the bad
54	  pattern has a *static signature in the artifact*. Where it does, it converts to a tech-pack
55	  check — a SAM `Handler` still carrying the entry's subdirectory under an esbuild build, an
56	  esbuild declared in `devDependencies`, a `SetIcon({path: …})`, a CloudFront custom
57	  origin-request policy listing `Authorization` — and the agent never needs to know the gotcha
58	  in advance: writing the bad pattern fails the check in the same session, moving discovery
59	  from runtime (often the first deploy or invoke) to write-time, with the gotcha's teaching in
60	  the failure message. Only the signature-less residue stays as skill knowledge: runtime
61	  divergence invisible in the artifact (jsdom *behaving* unlike Chrome, CORS being decided
62	  server-side) and diagnostic know-how. The release pack's **contract** is the
63	  largest signature-rich case — a conformance suite waiting to be written.
64	
65	## Architecture
66	
67	```
68	packs/                        # the mounted corpus: prose + checks, active by declaration
69	  registry.mjs                #   structural discovery — any packs/<name>/pack.mjs is a pack
70	  load-active-prose.mjs       #   SessionStart hook: emits active packs' RULES.md
71	  <baseline>/                 #   the baseline: RULES.md + the core checks (declared like any pack)
72	  <technology>/               #   coding gotchas (RULES.md, prose only)
73	  <technology>-release/       #   RELEASE.md (standard) + stubs + conformance checks (opt-in)
74	  <technology>/               #   the workflow lints (no prose)
75	  <technology>/  <technology>/  …      # more prose-only tech packs
76	  <project-class>/            #   a project-class pack (prose-only, declared)
77	checks/                       # the ENGINE only (runs the packs' checks)
78	  run.mjs                     #   dependency-free Node CLI
79	  lib/                        #   git diff scoping, findings format, markdown + manifest helpers
80	  stop-hook.mjs               #   blocks the agent's stop on blocking findings
81	  pretooluse-guard.mjs        #   blocks forbidden actions before they run
82	  test/                       #   fixtures (scratch git repos), red-first
83	packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/   # activity-scoped procedures, bundled in their owning pack
84	  checks.mjs                  #   the test-the-world checks that validate this skill's action
85	```
86	
87	**Skill-owned checks.** A skill defines the performance of an *action*; the test-the-world
88	check that validates that action's result belongs **beside the SKILL.md that defines it**, not
89	in a pack that owns none of the context. So a skill may carry its own checks — the
90	`routine-structure` check lives in its owning skill's folder, next to the routine-authoring
91	prose it enforces, with its test co-located too. A skill lives inside its owning pack
92	(`<pack>/skills/<name>/` — #385), so discovery IS the pack registry: any bundled skill's
93	`checks.mjs` (default export = an array of rules) is gathered onto the pack (`skillChecks`) and
94	runs when the pack is active. The pack gate only says the project opted into the pack — not
95	that this skill's action ever happened in this repo — so a skill check's `run` must still
96	**detect relevance first, cheaply and specifically, and return `[]` when
97	the artifact is absent** (`routine-structure` keys off a `routine.md` existing before it asserts
98	anything). Get that wrong and the check fires false findings on every unrelated repo the corpus
99	is mounted in. Reserve skill checks for the world-state a skill's action leaves behind; a rule
100	with no skill to anchor it stays a baseline check.
101	
102	**Where a check goes — the litmus test.** Classify by what the checked *artifact* is, not by
103	which doc teaches the fix (the `doc` pointer is where you *learn* the remedy — most baseline
104	checks point at a skill, so it is **not** the classifier):
105	
106	- present in ~every repo (markdown links, file layout, the root `CLAUDE.md`, git history, a
107	  branch's issue reference) → a **baseline** check;
108	- present only when a declared **technology** is (a workflow, a SAM template, the release
109	  stubs) → a **technology-pack** check, whose relevance is gated by declaration;
110	- present **only because one skill's discrete action created it** (a routine folder, from
111	  authoring a routine) → a **skill** check.
112	
113	Only the third — *the artifact would not exist had the action never run* — earns a home in the
114	skill. `routine-structure` is the sole current case: a routine folder exists only because
115	someone authored a routine. `squash-merge-history` points at the merge skill but stays
116	in the baseline, because git history exists in every repo and is disturbed by any merge, not only that
117	skill's action; `claude-md-length`, `generated-merge-driver`, and the placement check likewise
118	inspect artifacts every repo has, so they stay in the baseline despite naming a skill in `doc`.
119	
120	**Not every pack-machinery concern is a check.** The `.claudinite-checks.json` *settings* are
121	validated when the file loads, not by a conformance rule: malformed JSON, an unknown property,
122	and an unknown pack name are equally settings errors, surfaced by the runner as blocking `config`
123	findings. A pack's `marker` only *suspects* the pack is wanted — whether to declare it is the
124	project's call — so nothing checks that a declared pack carries its marker, or that a marker's
125	pack is declared. Pack **dependencies** (`requires`) are likewise resolved when the declaration is
126	*written* — bootstrap `--init` and the baselining backfill run `resolveDeclaredPacks` to pull each
127	declared pack's transitive `requires` into the file, materializing the prerequisite (like
128	the baseline) rather than nagging at every Stop. A materialized dependency is written as
129	`{ "id": ..., "via": [...] }` — `via` naming the declared packs that require it — so the file
130	itself records why the dependency is there.
131	
132	**Runner contract.** `node .claudinite/checks/run.js`. Dependency-free Node — no `npm install`
133	step exists on the tarball mount, and the corpus's own "earn each dependency" rule applies to
134	us first. Exit 0 = clean, exit 1 = blocking findings. The default scope is the **whole repo**:
135	on a text corpus the full sweep costs milliseconds, and only full scope sees cross-file
136	breakage — a change in one file dangling a reference in an unchanged one. The steady state is
137	a repo at zero findings (or reviewed acceptances), held there by every run. `--changed`
138	(diff vs the merge-base with main) exists only as a transitional aid while adopting a repo
139	that carries a backlog — it is not the enforcement default. (Rules that are inherently about
140	the *delta* — new suppression markers, commits referencing an issue — diff against the
141	merge-base in either scope.)
142	
143	**Pack selection: declared for deterministic execution, fingerprinted against drift.** The
144	packs a project runs are **pinned in `.claudinite-checks.json`**
145	(`"packs": ["baseline", "a-technology-pack", "a-release-pack"]`; no pack runs
146	undeclared — the baseline too is declared explicitly, seeded by bootstrap).
147	Execution is a closed, declared set: every rule in a declared pack
148	runs when its scope's surface runs — the work rules at the Stop hook, the world rules in the
149	test/CI flow — with no inference at execution time, so "the
150	project uses technology X" deterministically implies "every X check ran." Bootstrap writes the
151	initial declaration from the repo's fingerprint — a pack's `detect` marker (`.github/workflows/`
152	→ a workflow-lint pack; a `manifest.json` with `manifest_version` → the extension packs; the
153	release-workflow `name:`s → the conformance suite) seeds it at `--init`. But a marker only
154	*suspects* a pack is wanted: from then on the declaration is authoritative, and whether to add a
155	newly adopted technology's pack, or drop one whose technology has left, is the **project's** call
156	— the checker never second-guesses it. What *is* enforced is settings **validity**: an unknown
157	pack name, an unknown property, or malformed JSON is caught when the file loads
158	(`loadConfig` + the runner) and surfaced as a blocking `config` error — a wrong pack name is as
159	much a settings error as bad JSON. `.claudinite-checks.json` additionally holds per-rule
160	**overrides** and **acceptances** — at the top level for project-wide decisions, or on a pack's
161	own entry for the ones that pack's declaration motivates (see engine/checks/README.md).
162	
163	A declared id may name a **canon** pack or one of the repo's **own local packs**
164	(`.claudinite/local_packs/<id>/` — the project's tracked, project-specific packs, discovered from
165	the repo's own tree alongside the mounted canon; canonically declared by the namespaced token
166	`local_packs/<id>`, the bare id accepted while the fleet migrates — see engine/checks/README.md). Both
167	are the same closed-declared-set execution;
168	`knownIds` spans both, so a local id is valid, not an unknown-pack error, while a broken or
169	id-colliding local `pack.mjs` is surfaced as a blocking `config` finding rather than silently
170	dropping the pack's checks. A local pack's checks run when it is declared, exactly like a canon
171	pack's; this is where a project's *own* deterministic rules live (the checks-over-prose economy,
172	applied at the project's level) instead of always-loaded prose.
173	
174	**Acceptances are the escape hatch — deterministic and reviewable.** Rules with judgment
175	exemptions (a placement rule's "deliberate cross-cutting concern") need a way to say "yes, on
176	purpose" that isn't a fight with the hook: a per-finding `accept` entry with a mandatory reason
177	string, keyed by rule id + path. It lands in the diff like any code, so the *decision* gets
178	reviewed once instead of re-litigated every session. An acceptance a pack's adoption forces
179	lives on that pack's `packs` entry, so its provenance — which declaration required which
180	exception — is the file's own structure.
181	
182	An acceptance is a **check-the-world** instrument: a persistent, committed exemption a future
183	sweep keeps re-finding and must be told to ignore. It is the wrong tool for a **check-the-work**
184	finding — a conversation- or branch-scoped rule (e.g. `feature-requirements-first`) whose finding
185	a fresh session wouldn't even re-raise; accepting one leaves a permanent suppression for a
186	one-session artifact. Author a check-the-work rule to be **satisfiable by fixing the work, or to
187	self-skip** when its precondition isn't met (the spec it enforces against isn't in the repo, say):
188	a finding no correct work can clear forces the wrong remedy — an accept, or a post-hoc rebase —
189	so it's a bug in the rule, not a candidate for an acceptance.
190	
191	And when a rule mandates an **ordering** — X must happen before Y — it ships with a
192	check-the-work verification of that order, judged on the surface where the order is visible:
193	the conversation transcript (`feature-requirements-first`'s comment-scoped doc-first ordering)
194	or the branch commit log (a rule-before-fix test asserting the outlawing commit is an ancestor
195	of the fixing one, `pack-independence`'s pattern). A stated ordering with no check-the-work
196	verifier is prose-only enforcement — exactly what this system exists to replace.
197	
198	**The finding is the instruction.** This is the context economy of the whole design: the rule's
199	teaching text moves out of always-loaded context and into the failure message, paying its token
200	cost only on violation, in the session that violated it, pointed at the exact spot. Every
201	finding carries: rule id, `file:line`, what's wrong, *why* (one line — the model generalizes
202	from motivation), the fix, and a doc pointer for depth.
203	
204	<example>
205	
206	```
207	reference-distance  src/report/render.js:12
208	  imports ../../util/dates.js at distance 4.
209	  Why: the folder tree should encode the dependency graph; far reaches make it lie.
210	  Fix: move dates.js next to its users, lift it to a common ancestor, or accept it
211	       in .claudinite-checks.json with a reason if it's a deliberate cross-cutting util.
212	  More: .claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
213	```
214	
215	</example>
216	
217	## Enforcement wiring
218	
219	The two scopes fire at **different times**, because they answer different questions. The *work*
220	scope judges the change in front of the session and belongs on a per-turn hook; the *world* scope
221	is a whole-repo invariant assertion — the same shape as a test suite — and belongs wherever the
222	project runs its tests, not on every turn.
223	
224	**Work scope: a Stop hook is the guarantee; instructions are not.** Bootstrap registers one hook
225	in the consumer's `.claude/settings.json` (the same mechanism as the existing SessionStart hooks):
226	
227	1. The Stop hook fires when the agent finishes a turn.
228	2. It **fast-exits in milliseconds** when no tracked file differs from `main` — conversational
229	   turns cost nothing.
230	3. Otherwise it runs the **work** sweep (`check_the_work.mjs`, with the session transcript); on
231	   findings it exits 2 with them on stderr. Claude Code blocks the stop and feeds that text back
232	   to the agent, which fixes the violations **in the same session**. A clean run stops silently.
233	
234	Loop safety comes from convergence (fixed findings stop firing) plus Claude Code's own runaway
235	protection (it overrides a Stop hook after ~8 consecutive blocks).
236	
237	**World scope: wired into the project's test/CI flow (revises #385).** The whole-repo sweep runs
238	as its own step wherever the project runs its tests — a CI job, a `make test` target, an npm
239	script — invoked as the standalone `node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs`
240	command. It is deliberately **not** a language-specific test file (a `*.test.mjs` a Node runner
241	discovers): a Python/Rust/Go consumer's suite could not load one, and the sweep is the engine's
242	own always-vendored Node CLI, so it runs as a step in any flow regardless of the project's
243	language. Bootstrap wires this step during adoption, adding a minimal flow where the repo has
244	none. This **supersedes the original #385 decision** ("the Stop hook is the whole enforcement
245	surface; consumers ship no CI job"): the earlier design kept the world sweep on Stop to spare
246	consumers a CI setup, but running a whole-repo sweep every turn is work misplaced in time, and a
247	human editing on GitHub web (or any non-session tool) is now caught by the test/CI flow the
248	change lands through rather than by the next session's Stop.
249	
250	**The conversation surface (Stop hook only).** Some process rules leave their artifact not in
251	the repo but in the *session itself* — e.g. `comment-classification` (the reply to the owner's
252	latest comment must declare an explicit `Comment class:` line: the assessment stays judgment,
253	but that an assessment was made is checkable) and `feature-requirements-first` (a
254	feature-classified comment's doc-first ordering on the branch). The Stop hook is the one surface
255	that can carry these: Claude Code passes the hook `transcript_path` on stdin, the hook forwards
256	it as `--transcript`, and `ctx.conversation()` exposes the parsed session
257	([helpers/session-transcript.mjs](helpers/session-transcript.mjs)). Everywhere else — CI, a manual run — the transcript
258	is absent and these rules self-gate to `[]`, the same self-supplied relevance gate skill checks
259	use. Two scoping choices keep them convergent rather than nagging: only the *latest* owner
260	comment is judged (a transcript is append-only, so an old omission could never be fixed), and
261	the ordering rule scopes to commits after the comment's timestamp (earlier work on the branch is
262	never re-litigated). The Stop hook's clean fast path also means a purely conversational turn —
263	no tracked change vs the base — runs no checks at all, conversation rules included.
264	
265	**Prefer a platform setting when one exists — but never trust it.** Squash-only merging is a
266	GitHub repo setting; force-push protection is branch protection. The setting does the
267	*enforcing*, but it's configuration like any other: it can be off, get switched off, or be
268	bypassed, and nothing notices. So every setting rung pairs with a check that verifies it, in
269	order of strength:
270	
271	- **Effect check (preferred)** — offline and deterministic, it verifies the *outcome* the
272	  setting guarantees rather than the setting itself: squash-only ⇒ the change lands squashed,
273	  so its own commits carry no merge commit (`squash-merge-history` in the baseline pack). It
274	  is scoped to the work — the merge commits the current change introduces on HEAD's first-parent
275	  chain since the merge-base — not the repo's whole history: it catches the setting being off or
276	  bypassed *for this change* without re-auditing (and demanding acceptances for) legacy merges
277	  already on `main` that the work never touched. Testing the work, not the world, is what keeps
278	  the check from firing on every unrelated session.
279	- **Config check** — reads the setting via the platform API and fails when it's off. Needs a
280	  network-capable surface: rules carry a surface tag, the Stop hook runs only offline rules,
281	  CI runs what its repo token can read (e.g. the allow-merge-commit flags), and the fleet
282	  maintenance routine covers settings a repo token can't (e.g. branch protection). Follow-up
283	  work alongside the Phase 2 packs.
284	
285	## Governance
286	
287	- **A converted rule leaves its doc.** The check's failure message owns the rule now; the doc
288	  keeps only rationale and the judgment parts. Keeping both pays twice and springs the corpus's
289	  own drift trap (two sources of truth).
290	- **Fail fast: a new check ships at its real severity — blocking for defect-kind rules.** A
291	  wrong blocking check surfaces in the very next session and gets fixed; an advisory false
292	  positive is noise nobody reads, so a burn-in stage never actually observes the precision it
293	  waits for. The escape hatches bound a bad check's blast radius: a reasoned acceptance, a
294	  severity override, and the Stop hook's own two-block release. `advisory` remains a per-rule
295	  **kind**, not a stage — for rules whose own semantics are directional (a placement rule's
296	  metric is "a direction, not a hard gate"), where a finding is a smell to judge, not a defect
297	  to fix. Revisit delayed adoption only if the fleet grows people who can be hurt by a wrong
298	  block.
299	- **Telemetry drives retirement.** The runner logs firings; the fleet-maintenance routine
300	  already reads every vendored repo and can report "rules that never fired in N days" —
301	  obsolescence made measurable, the property instructions never had.
302	
303	## Skills — the on-demand layer for what checks can't carry
304	
305	Checks carry the *enforceable* rules. Everything else that today rides on soft pointers —
306	procedures, task-gated practices, technology knowledge — moves to **Agent Skills**, a mechanism
307	the system doesn't use yet. The docs' own decision rule fits exactly: *"Create a skill when …
308	a section of CLAUDE.md has grown into a procedure rather than a fact"*, and knowledge-bearing
309	skills are explicitly endorsed (*"reference content adds knowledge … conventions, patterns,
310	style guides, domain knowledge"*). The official hook-vs-skill line mirrors this design's ladder:
311	*"Use a hook when the action must happen the same way every time … Use a skill when Claude
312	should decide how to apply the steps, or when the content is knowledge rather than a script."*
313	
314	**What a skill buys over a CLAUDE.md soft pointer.** The token economics are roughly neutral —
315	a skill's name + description sit in context every session (progressive disclosure: the body
316	loads only on invocation), about what an index line costs today. The real gain is **trigger
317	reliability**: today a `tasks/` doc helps only if the agent remembers to follow the index line
318	("read before writing a test") — an instruction-following step that fails silently. Skill
319	matching is harness-managed and trained-for, skills are user-invocable as `/name` too (manual
320	invocation is deterministic — it runs when typed), and technology skills can be
321	**`paths`-scoped** (glob frontmatter) so they surface exactly when the matching files are
322	touched — a structural trigger, not a remembered one.
323	
324	Be clear about what this is *not*: **model-invocation of a skill is still probabilistic** —
325	better odds than a soft pointer, never a guarantee. That is precisely why this design's
326	division of labor puts nothing that *must* happen on a skill: enforcement lives in hooks,
327	checks, and settings, which are deterministic by construction; skills carry only guidance whose
328	worst-case miss is today's status quo. In particular, check execution never depends on skill
329	routing — the Stop hook runs the declared packs whether or not any skill fired. The split is
330	therefore **per-rule, not per-doc**: a doc's enforceable rules go to a pack (which runs
331	unconditionally for every project that declares it), its judgment residue rides the skill, and
332	there is deliberately no one-to-one correspondence between an instruction file and a pack. Two documented limits
333	to respect: keep descriptions tight (the listing truncates them, and the description budget
334	scales with the context window — many verbose skills degrade matching), and keep each
335	`SKILL.md` body well under 500 lines.
336	
337	### The catalog
338	
339	There is no skill catalog (#385): a skill is its owning pack's content
340	(`<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) — the pack's own README names what it bundles, and the
341	harness surfaces skills by their frontmatter descriptions, which is the routing.
342	
343	What stays always-loaded after this: a trimmed
344	baseline `RULES.md`, the judgment core of
345	the agent-practices skill (its trigger — "writing
346	code" — is near-universal, so a skill gains little; revisit with telemetry), and a much smaller
347	index. The routing index largely dissolves: routing *is what skill descriptions do natively*.
348	
349	### Delivery — incremental now, plugin end-state
350	
351	- **Now (works with both mount methods):** each skill is bundled in its owning pack
352	  (`<pack>/skills/<name>/`), and the SessionStart hook `engine/pack_loader/mount-skills.mjs`
353	  regenerates `.claude/skills/<name>` symlinks for the active packs' union each session —
354	  nothing committed (a committed link dangles on every plain checkout). Symlinked skill
355	  directories are documented, supported behavior, and skill changes are picked up live within
356	  a session — so mounts generated at session start still land, the same property the tarball
357	  sync populating their targets already relies on.
358	- **Later, maybe — Claudinite as a plugin (contingent on a spike).** A plugin is nothing
359	  exotic: a directory layout inside an ordinary git repo (`skills/`, `commands/`,
360	  `hooks/hooks.json`, a `plugin.json` manifest) plus a `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` that
361	  lets the repo serve as its own catalog. **No publication to Anthropic** — any git repo works
362	  as a marketplace directly, and the repo may carry arbitrary other content alongside the
363	  plugin dirs, so Claudinite would remain exactly the freely-amended GitHub repo it is (growth
364	  PRs, this doc, everything — unchanged). The draw: plugins bundle precisely this design's
365	  pieces — skills, commands, and hooks (SessionStart, Stop, PreToolUse) with bundled scripts
366	  addressable via `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` — and a consumer repo can commit
367	  `extraKnownMarketplaces` + `enabledPlugins` in `.claude/settings.json` to enable it for
368	  everyone. **Why it is not the plan of record:** the docs leave the operational questions that
369	  matter most to this system unanswered — how promptly consumers receive updates (manual
370	  `/plugin marketplace update` is documented; session-start auto-refresh is not), whether
371	  web/cloud sessions load marketplace plugins at all, and whether plugin hooks behave
372	  identically to settings-registered ones. A daily-growth corpus lives or dies on update
373	  latency, and the current SessionStart tarball sync *guarantees* latest-`main` every session.
374	  So: phases 1–4 ship entirely on the existing mount + symlinks and depend on the plugin route
375	  for nothing; adopt it only if a Phase-5 spike proves same-day propagation, web support, and
376	  hook parity. (Also documented: a plugin cannot inject always-on CLAUDE.md-style prose, so the
377	  residual baseline keeps its `@`-import either way.)
378	
379	## Growth pipeline: checks-first promotion
380	
381	New lessons enter the canon through the growth lifecycle (extract → promote → dedup). Today
382	the promote step generalizes a lesson and routes it to a prose doc.
383	Under this design, **prose becomes the fallback, not the default** — the point of promotion is
384	to relieve every project's context, and a check relieves it completely while prose only
385	relocates it.
386	
387	**The promotion ladder.** Every lesson that clears the worthiness bar is triaged down the same
388	mechanism order as the conversion table above — the *first* rung that can carry it wins:
389	
390	1. **Platform setting** — the platform enforces it outright, always paired with the check
391	   that verifies it holds (effect check first, config check where a token can read it).
392	2. **PreToolUse hook** — a bad action to block before it runs.
393	3. **Post-hoc check** — a constraint on repo state.
394	4. **Skill** — a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger.
395	5. **Prose canon** — only for what none of the above can carry, and the landing **names its
396	   reason** (judgment / in-flight behavior / platform knowledge), logged per lesson in the
397	   promote tracking issue so conversion rates are auditable.
398	
399	Concretely, three growth docs change:
400	
401	- **`item-routing.md`** gains a step 0: *mechanism triage*
402	  before file routing. "Which doc owns this" is only asked for lessons that fall through to
403	  rung 5.
404	- **`promote.md`**: for a rung-3 lesson, the routine authors
405	  the check in the same PR — rule id, detection, the failure message (which *is* the
406	  generalized lesson text), **plus a fixture proving it fires** on a violating input and stays
407	  quiet on a clean one (see-it-fail applies to checks too). When it can't produce a confident
408	  detection + fixture, it lands the lesson as prose **and** opens a tagged conversion-backlog
409	  issue — a visible miss to sweep later, never a silently-shipped broken check.
410	- **`dedup.md`**: a canon **check** covers a local prose item the
411	  same way a canon line does — better, since the coverage is enforced rather than stated. The
412	  runner exposes the rule catalog machine-readably (`run.js --list`: rule id, description,
413	  failure message, doc pointer); dedup quotes a **rule id** where it today quotes a canon line.
414	  This answers the obvious worry — "the canon won't have the instruction, only a test": the
415	  check *carries* its instruction as data (its failure message), so dedup compares against the
416	  catalog exactly as it compares against prose today, and more mechanically, since rule ids are
417	  stable where prose wording drifts. The keep-test is unchanged: a local item that says *more*
418	  than the check detects (a stronger point about a narrower case) stays.
419	
420	Extract is untouched: project-local capture stays prose at the project's own level —
421	conversion is a promotion-time judgment, made once, centrally.
422	
423	## Phasing
424	
425	1. **Runner + Stop hook + first baseline checks** — reference-integrity, task-lifecycle,
426	   warning-suppression (blocking); the placement check (advisory by kind). Bootstrap gains the
427	   hook-registration step.
428	2. **a workflow-lint pack + a release-conformance pack**, piloted on one
429	   extension repo.
430	3. **Baseline restructure** — the first skills (a merge recipe, a lessons pass) + the
431	   squash-only setting; temporary-workarounds → PreToolUse hook; slim the converted docs and
432	   the index.
433	4. **Skills layer + growth pivot** — the rest of the corpus (practice + technology skills,
434	   symlink delivery in bootstrap), and the promotion ladder lands in
435	   `promote.md`,
436	   `item-routing.md`, and
437	   `dedup.md`.
438	5. **(Contingent) plugin packaging** — only after a spike proves same-day update propagation,
439	   web-session support, and hook parity; until then the mount + symlink delivery is the plan of
440	   record and nothing depends on this phase.
441	6. **(Deferred)** LLM-judge checks in CI for judgment rules (naming, comment quality) —
442	   possible, but nondeterministic and token-costly; revisit only after 1–4 prove out.

1	# Extracting lessons from a working session
2	
3	> **Scope: a single agent ↔ user conversation.** This doc is the **method** for mining one
4	> working session's *dialogue and the actions taken in it* for improvements. It is **not** the
5	> growth extract ([extract.md](extract.md)) that mines **issues, PRs, and commits** over repo
6	> history — that routine never sees a conversation. Its two callers: the
7	> [conversation-extract daily task](conversation-extract.md), which applies it to **captured**
8	> conversation logs — where the friction signals below (a clarifying round-trip, a backtrack, a
9	> wait you sat through) survive with their timestamps — and an owner's occasional plain-words
10	> ask for a retrospective over the live session.
11	
12	Portable guidance for mining an agent ↔ user session — a Claude Code web session, a CLI run, a
13	captured conversation log — for durable improvements: read the conversation and convert its
14	friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less dependent on human
15	feedback.
16	
17	Run the reflection on a **capable model.** Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears
18	the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong
19	"lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
20	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model
21	to the judgment it must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the
22	separate efficiency analysis — also live there; this doc is the how-to.
23	
24	## The goal
25	
26	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less
27	rework, less waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but
28	as "where did this cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost
29	next time." If a pass can't name a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's
30	fine (see [No new lessons](#no-new-lessons-is-a-valid--and-common--result)).
31	
32	## When it runs
33	
34	Routinely, in the [conversation-extract daily task](conversation-extract.md) over each captured
35	log (a fresh pass within a day of capture, a final hindsight pass before retention deletes the
36	log) — the standard path. If an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective over the live
37	session, apply the same method and deliver the capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**,
38	never one that self-merges (the nightly auto-merges its own PR per its own doc; a live retrospective
39	wants human eyes). **Never
40	reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner
41	decides when a session is done enough to mine.
42	
43	## What to look for — the friction signals
44	
45	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop
46	cost more than necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
47	
48	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
49	
50	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I
51	meant…"); the agent building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same
52	request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
53	
54	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every
55	question the user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate
56	**convention or glossary entry**; a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first
57	checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc the agent reads cold and gets right the first
58	time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds correctly **without the round-trip**.
59	
60	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
61	
62	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran
63	a command that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light
64	one fit; reinvented something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written
65	to "verify"; missed an existing convention and had it corrected in review.
66	
67	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing
68	helper/convention so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read.** Place
69	it by where the trap is hit, not in a central bucket: a gotcha from **misusing a specific API,
70	class, or library goes as a comment right at the usage site** — next to the call itself, where
71	the next editor of that line sees it — never collected into a centralized gotchas list.
72	Co-locate it in a file's own header comment when the trap spans the whole file and you'd only
73	hit it *while editing that file*. Reserve a central gotchas doc for what no single usage site
74	owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant file (a mistake of omission), or a
75	cross-cutting invariant. The test: next time the agent takes the good path first, not after a
76	detour.
77	
78	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
79	
80	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been
81	parallel; a padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its
82	result was already in hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already
83	green.
84	
85	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers and separate the
86	kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting** (sleeps,
87	polling, a finished process not yet killed). A captured log carries per-entry timestamps and
88	per-message token usage, so the numbers are computable, not estimated. A fix is only credible
89	against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
90	was already optimal.
91	
92	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
93	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the
94	subject of the standing **efficiency analysis** in
95	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold a wall-time
96	finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
97	loss of quality.
98	
99	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
100	
101	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks
102	*repeatedly* are a checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how
103	many processes ran — could it be fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its
104	work was done?", stop waiting to be asked — fold those exact questions into a **standing
105	self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the relevant work, and close with a
106	terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each recurring question
107	converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
108	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively,
109	with numbers.
110	
111	## From signal to lesson — the bar
112	
113	A friction signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and
114	generalizable beyond this one session.** Before adding anything:
115	
116	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded
117	  differently, even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
118	- **Route to the local pack that owns it, and prefer the strongest mechanism** — the **local
119	  promotion ladder**, at the project's own level. A project's capture surface is its **local
120	  packs** (`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/`): pick the pack whose territory the lesson belongs
121	  to, then a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in that pack's `rules` (its failure message
122	  *is* the lesson; ship it with a red-first fixture), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a
123	  **pack skill**, and only what neither can carry lands as terse **prose** in the pack's
124	  `RULES.md`. Write more checks and less prose — a check relieves every session's context
125	  completely where prose only relocates it. A gotcha tied to one call site still goes as a
126	  comment at that site (above), not into any pack. When no pack's scope fits and the lesson
127	  warrants segregation, a new local pack is a self-contained directory drop.
128	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared,
129	  cross-project canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote
130	  stage lifts it there centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever
131	  travels.
132	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or
133	  something already implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
134	
135	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
136	
137	Most sessions yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write nothing
138	rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes
139	the canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a
140	genuinely new, reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.

1	# Prose-to-checks — sweep this repo's pack prose
2	
3	Mine the **existing** prose of this repo's packs — each pack's `RULES.md` / `SKILL.md` — for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Where [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md) descends the ladder for each *new* lesson, this task works the *backlog*: standing prose that was always mechanizable but never converted.
4	
5	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding scope**: it names the **pack paths** to sweep. Work only those paths — a consuming repo's own local packs by default; Claudinite also its core `packs/`. **Never** edit a read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.
6	
7	The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: convert prose to checks in a single owner-approved PR (a check can break CI or misfire, so it is reviewed, not auto-merged).
8	
9	## The method lives in the skill
10	
11	The conversion method — how to spot an always-testable rule in prose, judge convertibility, author the check plus its **see-it-fail** fixture, and decide what stays prose — is owned by the [**prose-to-checks** skill](../../skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md). Follow it; don't re-derive it here. This worker only frames the unattended run around it.
12	
13	## What a run does
14	
15	1. **Pick convertible prose** under the Context's pack paths — rules that are *always testable* (a deterministic condition a check could assert) and that no existing check already covers. Prefer the strongest, clearest candidates; converting one or two solid rules well beats churning many shakily.
16	2. **Convert per the skill** — author the rule module in its owning pack, register it in that pack's `pack.mjs`, and add a **fixture test that fires on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one** (see-it-fail is mandatory — a check that can't be made confident is left as prose, never shipped broken). Then apply the skill's **deletion test** to the prose the check now stands beside — a paragraph the check fully covers is deleted whole, never trimmed.
17	3. **Open a PR** — one PR for the run's conversions on a per-run-unique branch, its commit referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. Keep the repo's offline test suite green before opening.
18	4. **Log to the tracker** — the standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Prose to Checks`** in this repo. Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number**; create it already closed if missing. **Never open, close, or reopen it**. Log each run as a **dated comment**: the prose converted and the check id it became, or "nothing convertible this run".
19	
20	## What this task must never do
21	
22	- **Never ship a check that can't be made confident** — the see-it-fail fixture is the gate; an unprovable rule stays prose.
23	- **Never convert a rule an existing check already covers** — dedupe against the check set first.
24	- **Never touch a pack path outside the Context**, and **never edit a mounted canon pack** under `.claudinite/shared/` — a consumer improves only its own local packs.
25	- **Run on `opus`** — judging convertibility and authoring checks + fixtures is heavy judgment; this task declares `agent_model: opus`.

1	---
2	name: prose-to-checks
3	description: Mine a repo's existing pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, or when the growth prose-to-checks sweep runs.
4	---
5	
6	# Convert existing prose to checks
7	
8	A completeness-critic over a repo's own packs. The growth *extract* stage converts each **new**
9	lesson down the promotion ladder; this pass sweeps the **existing** prose backlog for rules that
10	are always-testable but still live only as prose — and converts them, so the packs keep shedding
11	context over time instead of only at the moment a rule is first learned. It runs as
12	grow_with_claudinite's daily `prose-to-checks-sweep` task, and on demand.
13	
14	## Scope — the pack paths you were given
15	
16	Work only the **pack paths configured for this repo** (the task passes them in its Context): a
17	consuming repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) by default — projects don't
18	improve core canon packs — while **Claudinite itself** also sweeps its core `packs/`. Read the
19	prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them). Never edit a
20	read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.
21	
22	## What to look for — the check-the-world test
23	
24	For each rule, ask the one question from
25	[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
26	signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**
27	
28	- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
29	  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
30	- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
31	  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
32	  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.
33	
34	The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
35	part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.
36	
37	## How to convert one
38	
39	Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
40	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:
41	
42	1. **Author the check** in the owning pack (`<pack>/<rule>.mjs`, listed in its `pack.mjs`) — the
43	   failure message *is* the rule (what / why / fix / `doc:` pointer back to the prose).
44	2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
45	   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
46	   doesn't ship.
47	3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory only when the rule is
48	   directional by kind.
49	4. **Delete the prose the check now covers** — whole, never trimmed. The deletion test below is
50	   how you decide which paragraphs those are.
51	
52	**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
53	its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
54	which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
55	*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
56	check to the same fixture bar.
57	
58	When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
59	candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.
60	
61	## Coming out: the deletion test
62	
63	Coming out of a conversion, apply the **deletion test**: prose a mechanism fully covers is
64	deleted, never trimmed. Ask it of every paragraph standing beside a landed check — *with this
65	paragraph gone, would the check still catch every violation it describes **and** tell the agent
66	how to fix it?* If yes, it is redundant: delete it whole. The check's failure message is where
67	the rule lives now and its header comment is where the rationale lives, so a paragraph restating
68	either pays twice and is the drift trap waiting to spring.
69	
70	Before concluding prose is the only carrier, look at the pack's **skills** too — an
71	activity-scoped skill often already holds the map a rule is repeating. Keep only what no artifact
72	carries.
73	
74	The test **discriminates** rather than just deleting: a paragraph stays whole whenever it carries
75	something the check does not — a second rule in the same breath, an exemption the check can't
76	encode, a value the check can't judge, or a remedy the finding's own `fix` line never states
77	(a finding renders `what` / `why` / `fix` / `doc`, never the rule's `description`, so a remedy
78	that lives only in the description is not carried). Two worked calls: an `npm test` invariant
79	went entirely — the check caught it and the testing-guide skill already listed the suites —
80	while an `extension-test/` mirror bullet stayed, because the check beside it enforced only the
81	`package.json` list's sync with the tree and never the mirror convention itself.
82	
83	Whether a check covers a rule is a judgment about meaning, so this test is applied by a
84	**reader**, not mechanized.
85	
86	## Bounds
87	
88	- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
89	  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
90	- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — the deletion test is only ever asked of a rule a
91	  *landed* check now enforces.
92	- Run the suite and the sweep green before opening the PR; open it for the owner's approval,
93	  never a direct push to `main`.

# The CANON repo's own CI — Claudinite's test suite + its own conformance sweep
# on every PR. Not consumer wiring (consumers ship no workflow, #385).
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  # Dispatchable so a GITHUB_TOKEN-authored PR (whose push/open GitHub never
  # turns into a pull_request run — the recursion guard) can still get this
  # suite started on its branch: baselining's deliver() and any bot flow like
  # migrations-retire's archive PR (#432, #565) dispatch it explicitly.
  workflow_dispatch:
defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash
jobs:
  test-and-conformance:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          # Check out the PR's real head, not the synthetic refs/pull/N/merge commit
          # actions/checkout uses by default — otherwise HEAD is an ephemeral merge of
          # the branch into main, which the work-scoped squash-merge-history check would
          # (correctly, for that synthetic commit) flag. This makes CI evaluate exactly
          # what the local Stop hook does: the branch tip. Falls back to github.sha on push.
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - name: Unit tests
        # THE test roots — a closed set of FOLDERS, each swept to any depth. Depth is
        # deliberately not enumerated: the previous form spelled out one glob per level
        # (`packs-tests/*/skills/*/*.test.mjs` and so on), so a test at an unlisted depth
        # was silently never run — which is exactly how vendoring/'s two files sat outside
        # CI. `**` removes depth from the question; what remains is the root list, and
        # engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs fails the moment a tracked test lands
        # outside it. Adding a root is a deliberate CI edit; adding a test is not.
        #   engine-tests/            engine/ + the other top-level canon code (migrations/, …);
        #                            mirrors engine/'s inner structure, and stays canon-side
        #                            because engine/ ships to consumers exactly as-is (#385)
        #   packs-tests/             every canon pack's tests, mirroring packs/
        #   vendoring/               co-located with the vendor computer/writer they cover
        #   dev/tools/               maintainer-side tooling nothing at session time runs
        #   .claudinite/local/packs/ this repo's own local packs — tests live inside the tree
        # nullglob: a root with no tests drops out instead of reaching node as a literal pattern.
        run: |
          shopt -s globstar nullglob
          tests=(engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs vendoring/**/*.test.mjs dev/tools/**/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs)
          node --test "${tests[@]}"
      - name: Conformance sweep
        # The world sweep's home is the test/CI flow (not the Stop hook, which
        # carries only the work scope) — this canon repo models the pattern
        # bootstrap wires into consumers. World only: the work scope judges a
        # session's change and runs at that session's Stop hook, not here.
        run: node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs
      - name: Promote write-surface gate
        # The growth promote stage (.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/tasks/growth-promote/task.md)
        # is the one change bounded to packs/ + skills/ — an ordinary engine PR legitimately edits
        # checks/ and engine/, so this cannot run on every PR. It keys on the promote branch prefix
        # (the task doc pins it) and fails the promote PR if a changed path strays.
        if: contains(github.head_ref, 'growth-promote')
        run: node .claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/promote-scope.mjs

1	# Python
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for a Python package built around an optional
4	heavy/native dependency (an ML model, a native audio/GPU library, a cloud SDK) that
5	most of the codebase — and the whole test suite — must run without. The theme is one:
6	**keep the importable core dependency-free, and gate every heavy thing behind an
7	optional extra.** What stays here is the architecture judgment that has no
8	false-positive-free static signature; the mechanical shape of the optional import
9	itself (imported lazily, guarded with an install-hint re-raise) is carried by the
10	`python-optional-deps` skill.
11	
12	## Keep the importable core dependency-free; heavy/native deps go in optional extras, not base `dependencies`
13	
14	The core of a package (its logic, storage, CLI, any web/dashboard layer) should import
15	and run — and be **fully testable** — with only the Python standard library. Declare
16	`dependencies = []` (or the genuinely-always-needed minimum) in `[project]`, and put every
17	heavy, native, or ML dependency under a **named `[project.optional-dependencies]` extra**
18	(`pkg[yamnet]`, `pkg[speaker]`, `pkg[dev]`). The test: if a `pip install <pkg>` with no
19	extra can't import the core, a heavy dependency has leaked into the base set — move it
20	to an extra.
21	
22	## Provide a stdlib-only implementation behind the same interface so tests and offline modes need no extra
23	
24	Give the swappable interface a **dependency-free** implementation — a scripted/mock
25	backend built on the standard library alone — alongside the heavy real one; that stdlib
26	backend is what the test suite and any offline/`simulate` mode run on. The heavy backend
27	is then just one more implementation of the interface, selected at runtime, never a hard
28	import the core or the tests depend on. The clean shape is a tiny backend interface plus
29	a `load_default()`/registry that lazy-imports the *selected* backend by name, so the
30	module that wires backends together never imports any of them at load time.
31	
32	## Mark the availability-probe import as a deliberate unused-import suppression
33	
34	An import kept **only** to probe whether an optional stack is present (its name is never
35	used directly — the code just branches on whether the import succeeded) is a real linter
36	false-positive for unused-import (`F401`). Mark that line `# noqa: F401` and record the
37	deliberate suppression, rather than deleting the probe or letting the warning ride.
38

1	# Web Speech APIs
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for browser voice I/O — speech-to-text
4	(`webkitSpeechRecognition` / the Web Speech `SpeechRecognition` API) and
5	text-to-speech (`chrome.tts` / `speechSynthesis`) — true for any app that reads
6	or listens through the browser, read cold. These are runtime browser-behaviour
7	gotchas, knowledge you carry into the code rather than state a tool can read off
8	the repo.
9	
10	> Some of these APIs (`chrome.tts`) are extension-only; where a rule touches
11	> MV3 service-worker / content-script mechanics, the general extension gotchas
12	> live in the [`chrome-extension`](../chrome-extension/RULES.md) pack.
13	
14	## Speech-to-text (`webkitSpeechRecognition` / Web Speech API)
15	
16	- **The recognizer owns its own microphone capture — you cannot hand it
17	  `getUserMedia` audio constraints.** `echoCancellation` / `noiseSuppression` /
18	  `autoGainControl` are `getUserMedia` *microphone* constraints, and the recognizer
19	  exposes no hook to set them on its internal stream (Chrome applies its default
20	  echo cancellation there regardless). To *warm* the device with a known processing
21	  state — and to read back whether echo cancellation actually engaged — run a
22	  separate preflight `getUserMedia({ audio: {…} })` capture and stop its tracks.
23	  (`suppressLocalAudioPlayback` /
24	  `restrictOwnAudio` are `getDisplayMedia` *screen-capture* constraints and have no
25	  bearing on a mic — don't reach for them here.)
26	- **Read the whole n-best list, not just alternative `[0]`.** Set
27	  `maxAlternatives` > 1 and iterate `result[0..length]` for `{ transcript,
28	  confidence }`; the ranked alternatives are exactly where homophone / near-miss
29	  recovery lives.
30	- **`onresult`, `onend`, and `onerror` all fire — settle the cycle exactly once.**
31	  Guard a `settled` flag: interim results arrive before the final one, a cycle can
32	  end with no result at all (treat `onend`-without-result as `no-speech`), and an
33	  error and an end can both arrive.
34	- **With `interimResults` off, engines omit `isFinal` — treat a result as final
35	  unless `isFinal === false`.** Don't test `if (result.isFinal)` (it's `undefined`
36	  on those engines and you'll drop every result); test `result.isFinal !== false`.
37	- **The classic recognizer streams audio to a cloud service (Google's) — plan for
38	  it.** A `network` error means "offline / service unreachable", and audio leaves
39	  the machine. On-device recognition is opt-in and capability-gated: probe
40	  `SpeechRecognition.available({ langs, processLocally: true }) === 'available'`
41	  once and cache it, set `recognizer.processLocally = true`, and **never trigger a
42	  language-pack download** (only `'available'` counts, not `'downloadable'`). When
43	  the local path is absent, fall back to ordinary cloud recognition unchanged.
44	- **Contextual biasing (`SpeechRecognitionPhrase` + `recognizer.phrases`) works
45	  only on the on-device path** — gate it behind that same availability probe and
46	  apply it best-effort (any failure falls back to un-biased recognition rather than
47	  breaking the listen cycle). Only bias **closed vocabularies you control**
48	  (a command lexicon, known labels, a spelling alphabet) with **modest** boosts:
49	  over-boosting makes the recognizer hear a biased phrase when the user actually
50	  said a same-sounding free-form utterance.
51	- **Map the raw Web Speech error names to a small taxonomy** — `not-allowed` /
52	  `service-not-allowed` → permission-denied, plus `no-speech`, `network`,
53	  `aborted`, `audio-capture`, else `other`. In particular `aborted` is the
54	  *self-inflicted* stop (you called `recognizer.abort()`), so the caller should
55	  ignore it rather than surface it as a failure.
56	- **A missed endpoint mid-utterance needs a pause watchdog, not just `onend`.**
57	  If interim hypotheses exist but no final arrives, the engine may have lost the
58	  endpoint; a timer that fires after a pause discards the half-heard input and
59	  reopens a fresh cycle (preventing "heart heart" doubles when the user repeats
60	  themselves). Set the threshold **well above a natural mid-command thinking
61	  pause** — a tight window (~1.2 s) cuts real commands; a wider one (~1.8 s) keeps
62	  only the genuine missed-endpoint case.
63	- **Mic permission is per-origin, and the grant belongs to whatever page the
64	  recognizer runs in.** In a content script the prompt reads as the *host site*
65	  asking and the grant persists for that origin. Surface it in a controlled moment:
66	  preflight `navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'microphone' })`, then a one-time
67	  `getUserMedia` to raise the prompt. **Retry the capture bare** (`{ audio: true }`)
68	  if the first constrained call is rejected — a browser balking at the constraint
69	  *shape* must not be misread as a permission denial; only a second failure is a
70	  real "denied".
71	
72	## Text-to-speech (`chrome.tts` / `speechSynthesis`)
73	
74	- **Prefer `chrome.tts` over `speechSynthesis` — it's immune to page
75	  autoplay / user-activation gating.** `speechSynthesis` invoked from a content
76	  script is subject to the host page's autoplay policy and can silently refuse to
77	  speak; `chrome.tts` (extension-only, needs the `"tts"` permission, usable from the
78	  service worker) is not. Make `chrome.tts` primary and `speechSynthesis` the
79	  fallback for non-extension document contexts.
80	- **`chrome.tts` doesn't exist in a content script — relay speak/cancel to the
81	  service worker over a port.** Keep the same `speak()`/`cancel()` contract on both
82	  sides; the in-page port sends `{ speak }` / `{ cancel }` messages and the worker
83	  drives `chrome.tts`. On port disconnect, resolve every pending `speak()` promise
84	  so a dead worker never leaves the caller awaiting an utterance that will never
85	  finish.
86	- **Voice lists load lazily — an empty `getVoices()` means "not ready yet", not
87	  "no voices".** Resolve the preferred voice on the *first* `speak()` and don't
88	  cache an empty result: fall back to the default that turn and try to resolve
89	  again next turn.
90	- **Don't trust the OS/browser default voice — it's often the most robotic one
91	  installed.** Keep an ordered list of preferred voice names, take the first one
92	  actually installed, and fall back to the default only when none match.
93	- **Resolve a `speak()` promise on *any* terminal event, and never reject.** For
94	  `chrome.tts` that's `end` / `interrupted` / `cancelled` / `error`; for
95	  `speechSynthesis` it's `onend` / `onerror`. Resolving (not rejecting) on error
96	  keeps a spoken-prompt sequence from deadlocking on one bad utterance. Use
97	  `enqueue: false` so a new line interrupts the current one for turn-taking rather
98	  than stacking up.
99	- **Neither engine reliably supports SSML — you can't force intonation.** If a
100	  punctuation cue matters (a question's rising tone), speak the cue in words
101	  ("question mark") rather than relying on prosody the engine may not apply.

1	# Flutter
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for Flutter / Dart codebases — true for any Flutter project
4	read cold. Earned in missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers (a Firebase-backed, location-driven app with an
5	executable-requirements UI suite); keep anything project-specific in the consuming repo's docs.
6	
7	## Architecture: ports out of the widget tree
8	
9	- **Widgets depend on ports, never on plugins.** Every platform/backend concern (location, auth,
10	  push, backend calls, the clock) enters the UI as a hand-written abstract interface with pure-Dart
11	  value types; plugin adapters (`geolocator`, `firebase_*`, `google_sign_in`, …) implement them and
12	  are constructed **only** in `main.dart`. A plugin type leaking into a screen (a geolocator
13	  `Position`, a `FirebaseFunctionsException`) is a defect: it silently couples every widget test to
14	  the plugin's platform channels.
15	- **Enforce the boundary with a committed import-scan test** (dart:io over `lib/ui/`, `lib/screens/`
16	  looking for forbidden import prefixes). The analyzer won't stop a convenient leak.
17	- **Ship the fakes in the package** (`lib/testing/`): scripted fakes for each port that also
18	  *record* what the UI asked of them, plus a `FakeWorld` bundling them with a pinned clock and the
19	  real app shell. Both the app's own tests and any sibling test package (e.g. an
20	  executable-requirements suite) import one fake world — never two parallel ones.
21	- **Extract the root shell into a widget** (`lib/app.dart`) taking the ports as parameters, used
22	  identically by `main.dart` (adapters) and the test harness (fakes). Tests must never rebuild a
23	  parallel MaterialApp — actuals come from the shipped shell.
24	- **Inject the clock.** Any widget that formats or compares times takes a `Clock` port; relative
25	  time rendered from `DateTime.now()` is untestable and drifts goldens.
26	
27	## Widget tests and goldens
28	
29	- **Load real fonts before any golden** — the test binding defaults to the glyph-less Ahem stub
30	  (text renders as boxes). Parse `FontManifest.json` from the root bundle and `FontLoader` every
31	  family (strip the `packages/<pkg>/` prefix so plain family names resolve), which also loads
32	  MaterialIcons; bundle text faces (e.g. Roboto) in the test package's pubspec. Watch for styles
33	  that don't inherit the theme's family — `ButtonStyle`/`styleFrom` text styles are the classic
34	  leak; pin `fontFamily` there explicitly.
35	- **Never `pumpAndSettle` around indeterminate progress indicators** — they schedule frames
36	  forever and the call never returns. Use fixed-duration pumps (`pump()` then
37	  `pump(Duration(...))`); this also makes an in-flight state (a spinner mid-send) a deterministic,
38	  golden-capturable frame. Corollary: after `tap()`, pump **twice** — one frame applies state, the
39	  fixed-duration pump advances implicit animations (ink ripples, color lerps) past the capture.
40	- **Anything that fetches must be injectable**: map tile providers, avatar images. Widget tests
41	  block real HTTP (a 400-returning stub client), so a `NetworkImage`/network `TileProvider` in the
42	  tree means error boxes, not screenshots. Provide a deterministic in-memory substitute (a
43	  canvas-drawn `ImageProvider` works and needs no asset files).
44	- **Fix the viewport per suite**: set `tester.view.physicalSize` and `devicePixelRatio` to one
45	  phone-shaped size (and reset in teardown) so layout — and therefore goldens — can't drift with
46	  the harness default.
47	- **Async lifecycle guards need an epoch counter.** A `start()` that awaits (permission check,
48	  first fix) can re-arm streams/timers after `stop()`/dispose ran mid-await; bump an epoch in
49	  `stop()` and bail after every await if it changed. The symptom (leaked GPS subscription after
50	  sign-out) is invisible in tests that don't await realistically.
51	
52	## Toolchain habits
53	
54	- **Verify plugin APIs against the installed source, not memory.** Major Flutter plugins break
55	  their APIs often (google_sign_in v7's `authenticate()`, flutter_map v7+'s options, geolocator's
56	  settings objects); resolved versions live in the pub cache
57	  (`~/.pub-cache/hosted/pub.dev/<pkg>-<ver>/lib/`) — read them before writing against them.
58	- **`pubspec.lock` moving without `pubspec.yaml` moving is version skew, not a dependency change.**
59	  An app commits its lockfile (only a *library* package gitignores it), so the file is tracked on
60	  purpose — the thing to keep out of the diff is the churn a local `flutter pub get` produces when
61	  the installed SDK resolves differently from CI's. Unless you deliberately ran an upgrade, revert
62	  it: `git checkout -- pubspec.lock`.
63	- **`flutter analyze` at zero issues** (infos included) is the bar a suite holds; lints that fight
64	  a deliberate convention (e.g. `file_names` vs. leaf-id case filenames) get disabled narrowly in
65	  that package's `analysis_options.yaml` with the reason as a comment.
66	- **Sandboxed/CI runners**: `flutter test` can stall for minutes at teardown on GPU-less containers
67	  with dropped sockets. The pattern that holds: stream output, kill the process group the moment
68	  the definitive marker prints (`All tests passed!` / `Some tests failed`), watchdog-kill on output
69	  silence. On healthy machines plain `flutter test` is equivalent — keep the wrapper thin.
70	- **The web sandbox ships no Flutter SDK.** Claude Code on the web boots without Flutter, so tests,
71	  `flutter analyze`, and golden regen can't run until it's installed. Install belongs in the
72	  environment **image** (built once, snapshotted, reused) — never a per-session hook that reinstalls
73	  every start. This pack declares that need in its `env` block ([pack.mjs](pack.mjs)); a project pastes
74	  one generic `environment-setup-command.sh` that runs every active pack's requirement via
75	  [engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs](../../engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs) and asserts it at session start (see [bootstrap.md](../../bootstrap.md)
76	  Part 9).
