1	# Spec-Driven Product Working Procedures — a portable playbook
2	
3	This document defines **how the owner wants a spec-driven product project run**, as a **bootstrap to
4	drop into a new project of this class** from day one. The class: **build and ship a small end-user
5	product against an executable specification — every requirement is a numbered leaf claimed by exactly
6	one executable proof of the right kind, expected results are owned by the owner, and releases cut
7	automatically while `main` stays green.** The archetype is a UI-centric product (a browser-extension
8	panel, a small web or mobile app) and the examples lean that way, but the discipline applies wherever
9	observable behavior can be specified leaf by leaf — read "surface", "render", and "server" as whatever
10	they mean for your project.
11	
12	It is written to be project-agnostic: it carries the durable working procedures and none of the
13	product, stack, or harness specifics of any particular project. Those live elsewhere — platform
14	gotchas in the project's technology packs, release mechanics in its release pack or release doc, and
15	the concrete spec, harness, and commands in the project's own docs. General test-trust practices
16	(see-it-fail, snapshot hygiene, the re-baselining approval procedure, capture-artifact-first) are
17	corpus canon in the writing-tests skill; this pack assumes them and adds the class's development loop
18	on top.
19	
20	Treat it as a **default to adapt, not a contract**: when a rule here doesn't fit, say why and drop it;
21	when the project needs a rule this document lacks, add it in the project's own docs first. The
22	non-negotiable is the spirit: **the spec is executable, the expecteds belong to the owner, the real
23	code produces every actual, and the product ships on green.**
24	
25	---
26	
27	## 1. The executable spec is the backbone
28	
29	- **One numbered requirements document states what the product must do**, leaf by leaf: what each
30	  surface must render, how it must behave, the exact copy and semantics it must carry. Not prose
31	  aspirations — specific, testable statements.
32	- **Keep the spec's boundary crisp: a leaf is what the harness can assert.** The feature-level story —
33	  what the product does and why — lives in the product's prose docs; the spec holds the specific,
34	  testable statements (exact strings, placement, semantics). A statement no kind can prove isn't a
35	  leaf yet: it stays prose, or it's the trigger to add the kind that can prove it.
36	- **Every leaf carries a stable id.** Add new requirements under new numbers; never renumber or reuse
37	  a retired one — the ids are what cases, commits, and review discussion key on.
38	- **Doc-first, red by default.** Adding a leaf with no executable proof fails the build until a case
39	  claims it.
40	- **The spec drives the tests, never the other way around.** A behavior change starts by editing the
41	  leaf, watching the gate go red, then changing product and proof to match. A test changed without its
42	  leaf — or a leaf reworded to match what the code happens to do — inverts the authority.
43	
44	## 2. Every leaf ⇄ exactly one proof, of the right kind
45	
46	- **Enforce the bijection with a committed coverage gate**: each leaf claimed by exactly one case,
47	  each case claiming exactly one leaf, and every discovered kind of case actually executed by a
48	  runner. The gate is part of the project's own suite.
49	- **A *kind* is one way a requirement can be asserted** — a rendered-state snapshot, a driven gesture,
50	  a pure rule, a boundary-enforced rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually observe what it
51	  asserts. Keep kinds **extensible** — adding one is a self-contained drop.
52	- **A kind may be a singleton.** "The product loads in the real environment" is a perfectly good leaf
53	  whose mechanism is one end-to-end case; the kind names the *way of asserting*, not a population of
54	  cases.
55	- **Give each kind's runner a named lane, and keep the default lane fast and deterministic.** Heavy
56	  real-environment kinds gate the merge from CI without slowing the inner loop; their trust rules
57	  (twice-green before merging, self-diagnosing on failure) are canon in the writing-tests skill.
58	- **Actuals come from the real code.** Whatever the kind, the proof drives the shipped entry points
59	  under a faithful harness — never a parallel re-implementation of what production "should" do (the
60	  writing-tests skill owns the general rule).
61	
62	## 3. Expected results are owner-owned
63	
64	- **The committed expecteds are the owner's approval record of the product.** A case's success
65	  criterion encodes what the owner accepted.
66	- **The contract takes two honest shapes.** *Artifact-expected* (a committed render, an exact-values
67	  file): the owner approves a committed file — an agent may **propose** the expected for a brand-new
68	  leaf, but never modifies a committed one to make a failing case pass. *Coded-expected* (an
69	  assertion, a `verify()`): the expected **is** the assertion — keep it outside the write surface of
70	  whatever writes the product code, so passing by weakening the check isn't even expressible.
71	- **On a mismatch, surface actual vs. expected (and the diff) and ask.** The re-baselining procedure —
72	  diff shown, owner approves, only then re-baseline — is canon in the writing-tests skill, and it
73	  applies uniformly: to a moved render, a changed values file, and a failing assertion alike.
74	- **Expected changes ride the normal review flow** — they land in the diff like code, so the owner
75	  approves the product change and its new expected together, once.
76	
77	## 4. State a requirement once; prove it at every boundary that enforces it
78	
79	- **A product rule with more than one enforcing tier gets sibling leaves under one statement** — e.g.
80	  "only signed-in users can post": the surface's half (the client sends credentials) and the
81	  boundary's half (the server rejects an unauthenticated write) are separate proofs of one
82	  requirement.
83	- **The proof lives where the rule is actually enforced.** A surface-side test of a server-enforced
84	  rule proves only that the client cooperates, not that the boundary holds; if the real enforcement is
85	  the backend, a leaf must exist there, exercised against the real handler.
86	
87	## 5. A supported-targets matrix is spec, not folklore
88	
89	- **When part of the product's value is breadth over external targets** — supported sites, file
90	  formats, providers, locales — each supported target is its own leaf, so dropping a target is a
91	  visible spec change, not a silent regression.
92	- **Prove each target against a committed, real sample of it** (a captured page, a genuine file), with
93	  the owner-reviewed exact-values expectation committed beside it — capture the sample first and read
94	  the expecteds off the committed bytes (canon in the writing-tests skill). A hand-invented sample
95	  proves support for a target the world doesn't actually serve.
96	- **Adding a target is a documented, repeatable flow** that lands the new leaf, its real sample, and
97	  its reviewed expected together.
98	
99	## 6. Green means "claimed", not "fully verified" — track the gap honestly
100	
101	- **Say what the harness cannot reach, naming the exact boundary of each stub.** A faithful harness is
102	  still a model of the platform; the honest sentence pattern is "this proof confirms our code *asks*
103	  for the action, not that the platform *performs* it". Put that statement where readers of the spec
104	  will see it — a banner on the requirements doc, linking the issue that tracks closing the gap —
105	  rather than in a test README footnote.
106	- **Deliberate gaps are marked at the leaf and committed, never remembered.** A leaf that can't be
107	  faithfully verified yet stays in the spec, visibly provisional (a loud "to be decided" marker, and a
108	  pointer to whatever covers it meanwhile), and is listed in a committed allowlist the coverage gate
109	  checks — the allowlist is the burn-down list, shrunk deliberately. Prefer a real validation; reach
110	  for the marker only for a genuinely undecided edge case or a not-yet-wired harness.
111	
112	## 7. The owner reviews the product surface, not the internals
113	
114	- **Embed regenerated renders of the real states in the spec itself** — the requirements document
115	  doubles as a gallery of what the product actually shows, generated from the shipped code, so
116	  approving the spec *is* approving the product's appearance.
117	- **Regenerate, never hand-edit.** The gallery is derived output of a committed generator; fixing it
118	  means fixing the source (or the generator) and regenerating.
119	- **The deterministic golden-image method this leans on is canon in the writing-tests skill** —
120	  matching the render engine to the surface (a bit-exact rasterizer for inline-styled/SVG surfaces, a
121	  headless browser for pages that use grid/vars/emoji/form-widgets), bundled fonts, capturing a
122	  host-page surface with styles inlined, and a drift gate on the embedded gallery.
123	
124	## 8. Ship automatically while `main` stays green
125	
126	- **`main` is releasable at all times, and automation does the releasing** — a release (and, where
127	  the platform has one, store publication) cuts from `main` on its own cadence without a human build
128	  step. Keeping `main` green *is* the release gate: a red `main` is a shipping outage, fixed before
129	  new work.
130	- **The version users see moves deliberately.** Automation may patch-bump to ship, but a meaningful
131	  version change is a decision made on `main`, not a side effect. The concrete release contract —
132	  workflows, artifacts, store procedures — belongs to the project's release pack or release doc, not
133	  here.
134

1	# Node.js
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for working in Node.js / npm codebases — package management, scripts, module resolution, runtime gotchas — true for any Node project read cold.
4	
5	## Module resolution
6	
7	- **A *named* import from a package's CommonJS entry can silently yield `undefined`.** Node recovers named bindings from a CJS module by static analysis, and that analysis fails on plenty of real entry points (a re-export built at runtime, a conditional assignment) — with no error: the import resolves, the binding is `undefined`, and the failure surfaces later as "x is not a function". When a package ships both entries, import the **ESM** one explicitly (`…/package/index.mjs`, or the `import` condition of its `exports`) for named bindings; when it doesn't, `import pkg from '…'` and destructure off the default. Resolve the package's own directory (`$(npm root -g)/<pkg>` for a global install) rather than hardcoding an absolute path into a version-pinned layout, which moves under you on the next image or upgrade.
8	- **Modern Node (22.7+) detects ES-module syntax in a `.js` file on its own** — no `"type": "module"`, no flag, no warning. A directory of ES modules therefore needs **no `package.json` of its own** just to be loadable; adding one to declare module-ness is cargo cult, and one already present for that reason is vestigial. (Prefer `.js` consistently within a tree over mixing in `.mjs` for the same purpose; the extension is then a style choice, not a signal.)
9	
10	## jsdom diverges from a real browser in ways a green test can hide
11	
12	Two that recur:
13	
14	- **`body.innerText` is null in jsdom.** Code reading `el.innerText || el.textContent` therefore falls through to `textContent` under test, which *includes* the `<script>` / `<style>` text, `<select>` / `<option>` text, and CSS-hidden text a real browser's `innerText` omits. Treat body-text results as jsdom-optimistic; never add a test that only passes because of it.
15	- **`runScripts: "outside-only"` (the default) parses `<noscript>` into live DOM — the opposite of a real browser.** A `textContent` read looks clean under test but splices the `<noscript>` markup into the value in Chrome, which keeps `<noscript>` as raw text. Parse a script-free fragment with `runScripts: "dangerously"` to reproduce the browser.
16

1	# Working discipline
2	
3	The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.
4	
5	Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.
6	
7	Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix.
8	
9	1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
10	2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
11	3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.
12	
13	The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.
14	
15	Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.
16	
17	When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.
18	
19	When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."
20	
21	Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.
22	
23	Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.
24	
25	Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.
26	
27	When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.
28	
29	An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.
30	
31	# The task lifecycle
32	
33	The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.
34	
35	For every new task:
36	
37	1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
38	2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
39	3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.
40

1	# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy
2	
3	The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
4	pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
5	the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
6	([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
7	[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
8	[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).
9	
10	The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**
11	
12	- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
13	  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
14	  ref's auto-generated name.
15	- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
16	  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
17	  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
18	  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.
19	
20	Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
21	**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
22	rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
23	three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.
24

1	# Claudinite — the canon's own non-portable working rules
2	
3	This is the Claudinite home repo's own local pack: the capture surface for lessons that are
4	**specific to working on the canon itself** and would not make sense mounted into a consuming
5	project. Portable lessons — anything true for repos beyond this one — belong in the shared canon
6	under `packs/`/`skills/` instead (proposed by PR, or lifted by the promote stage).
7	
8	The growth lifecycle writes here automatically: the `growth-extract` and `conversation-extract`
9	daily tasks route the canon's own non-portable lessons into this pack (each at the local
10	promotion ladder's strongest mechanism — a check where the rule is deterministic, otherwise terse
11	prose below).
12	
13	## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate
14	
15	- **`canon-curation` lives in `.claudinite/local/packs/`, not `packs/`** (owner decision,
16	  2026-07-19). The canon home's curation duties are Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite —
17	  project-specific content on the home's own capture surface. Do not propose moving it back, and
18	  do not describe the move as open or provisional.
19	- **Local-pack `run_daily` scheduling is ON — the fleet's default path** (same decision). The
20	  planner reads every member's local-pack daily descriptors by default; never reintroduce an
21	  "experimental / not enabled" framing or an opt-in seam for it.
22	- **Packs-tree segregation is barriers configuration only.** Any rule about what the `packs/`
23	  tree may reference is expressed by declaring/configuring the `barriers` pack (contributed
24	  edges, `siblings`/`scope` capabilities — extend barriers generically if a capability is
25	  missing). Never write standalone code that checks packs-tree segregation.
26	- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` records the mechanism only** (owner decision, 2026-07-23,
27	  #420). Status, phase tracking, in-flight-PR reconciliation and remaining work live in that
28	  initiative's tracking issue (agent-preprocessing → #394); a phased plan lives in the sibling
29	  `MIGRATION.md`. Don't reintroduce a status / open-questions / remaining-work section there.
30	- **Multi-session work hands off through the tracking issue, never a prepared prompt** (owner
31	  correction, 2026-07-23). The owner's opener is `continue work on #<n>`, so state not written
32	  into the issue is lost. Before ending a session on unfinished work, update the issue and let
33	  the session summary be a pointer to it — never compose a bespoke "pick up from here" prompt.
34	- **The canon never knows which repos consume it — fleet-wide aggregation is Sheepdog's domain**
35	  (owner correction, 2026-07-28, #520). Designing anything that spans repos, the tempting shape is
36	  a member list (or a "fleet" task) living in the canon. It doesn't go here: the canon carries only
37	  **mechanisms exercised on itself**, and the knowledge of *which* repos exist stays in the
38	  **Sheepdog** repo and its pack, which enumerates members at runtime from its own
39	  `.claudinite-checks.json` entry — exactly where `fleet-census` and `fleet-freshness` already keep
40	  it. So a cross-repo feature splits in two: a self-contained per-repo half in the canon, and the
41	  aggregation half as a Sheepdog fleet task. **No repo list exists anywhere in canon code** — and a
42	  derived fleet artifact lands in Sheepdog as a daily **auto-merged PR of a `GENERATED` file**,
43	  never a direct commit to its `main`.
44	- **A pack default stays in the pack — don't ask it at adoption, don't write it into a member's
45	  config** (owner ruling, 2026-07-28, #527/#528). An adoption question whose recommended answer is
46	  right for nearly everyone is "bad noise": it taxes every adopting repo to re-state the default,
47	  and materializing that answer into `.claudinite-checks.json` freezes a copy that then drifts from
48	  the pack and has to be migrated. Keep the default in the pack's own code, ask nothing, and let the
49	  rare project that wants to differ add the setting by hand. Read config as *optional* — an unset
50	  key means "the default", never "misconfigured" (`retention_days` unset is precisely why the
51	  conversation-extract prune is skipped rather than failing).
52	
53	## Canon-specific gotchas
54	
55	- **Baselining backfill skips the home.** The nightly baselining that lands a `seededByDefault`
56	  pack (and canon-delivered declaration changes) on every member is gated `!isHome`, so the canon
57	  home is the one repo it never reaches: what the fleet receives automatically, this repo's own
58	  `.claudinite-checks.json` only ever gets by hand.
59	- **The home doesn't declare `git-github`, so its skills never mount — never conclude "no such
60	  skill" from `.claude/skills/`.** `mount-skills.mjs` filters on the *literal* declaration
61	  (`isActive(p, { packs: declared })`), not the `requires` closure `check_the_world.mjs` resolves,
62	  and the baselining that would normalize that closure into `.claudinite-checks.json` is the one
63	  thing gated `!isHome` — so `merge-to-main` and `git-github-advanced` are simply absent here.
64	  Read `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` out of the tracked tree — the corpus *is* this repo,
65	  and an unmounted skill says nothing about whether its procedure applies. The seeding gap above
66	  is a different one (`git-github` arrives by closure, never `seededByDefault`); catching this
67	  one needs `resolveDeclaredPacks` compared against the literal declaration.
68	- **Never re-serialize a repo's JSON config to apply an edit — patch the text.** A round-trip
69	  rewrites what it wasn't asked to: Python's `json.dump` defaults to `ensure_ascii=True` (every
70	  non-ASCII character becomes a `\uXXXX` escape), and indent, key order and the trailing newline
71	  become the serializer's opinion. Nothing fails and tests stay green, so it rides onward. Edit
72	  JSON as anchored text; if you must round-trip, pin every lossy default and read the resulting
73	  diff before committing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `repo-text-sweeps`, where a
74	  `\uXXXX`-in-tracked-JSON check would carry it.)
75	- **Test git fixtures must commit with signing off.** `engine-tests/helpers.mjs`'s `makeRepo`
76	  overrides identity but not signing, so all 31 call sites route fixture commits through the
77	  signing service; when it degrades, each commit blocks on it and the suite leaks descriptors
78	  (~800 per full run against a 4096 cap) until `git commit` and `git push` fail process-wide.
79	  Commit with `git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit --no-gpg-sign`: signing a tmpdir throwaway
80	  buys nothing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `writing-tests`.)
81	- **A canon session with a consumer repo also in its sources will reach for the *consumer's*
82	  merge skill — merge by the skill of the repo you are merging into.** Canon work is routinely
83	  dual-repo (the canon plus the fleet member being piloted), and both repos ship a merge skill
84	  under different names — the canon's `packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/` and, say, GCEC's
85	  local `merge-and-ci`. The consumer's skill wins the match on name/description and is followed
86	  to the letter, so the canon-only steps in *its* recipe are silently skipped — repeatedly, the
87	  **post-merge conversation capture** (`node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue
88	  <n>`, the "After the merge" section of `merge-to-main`). So: before merging in a dual-repo
89	  session, resolve the merge skill **by target repo**, not by which skill matched first — and
90	  treat capture as part of the merge, not as an optional epilogue.
91	- **Fail-soft SessionStart steps hide their own breakage fleet-wide — test the emitted
92	  output, not the exit code.** Every `engine/pack_loader/` SessionStart step
93	  (`inject-pack-prose.mjs`, `mount-skills.mjs`, `env-requirements.mjs`) wraps its body in
94	  `try { ... } catch {}` so a broken loader never blocks a session. That fail-soft is deliberate,
95	  but it means a runtime fault — a wrong dynamic-import target, a renamed module — exits 0 and
96	  simply emits nothing: no error, no signal. And because the engine is vendored verbatim into
97	  every member, one canon regression silently disables that step across the whole fleet at once.
98	  So a step like this must be guarded by a regression test that runs the real script against a
99	  real corpus and asserts the **positive** effect — prose IS emitted — never merely that
100	  `status === 0` (which fail-soft makes meaningless); see
101	  `engine-tests/pack_loader/inject-pack-prose.test.mjs`.
102	- **The nightly self-refresh cannot repair the vendor-set computation — pin operational
103	  files against the REAL canon tree.** Baselining's converge re-runs
104	  `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.mjs` from canon HEAD, so a bug *in that computation* is
105	  the one class of canon regression that is not self-healing: every refresh faithfully
106	  reproduces it, and recovery is an out-of-band vendor refresh applied to each member by
107	  hand. So when the vendor set excludes by *pattern*, an operational file that matches
108	  needs a by-path whitelist (`VENDORED_ENGINE_DOCS`) **and** a regression test asserting
109	  against the real canon tree, not only a synthetic fixture: a fixture keeps proving the
110	  whitelist mechanism works while the live path silently drops out from under it (see the
111	  paired tests in `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.test.mjs`).
112	- **You cannot force a due slot by running the scheduler workflow by hand.** Dueness is
113	  stateless — a slot is due iff its time falls in `(last successful run, now]` — so a
114	  `workflow_dispatch` run outside the slot's window succeeds, prints `- no tasks due`, and
115	  does nothing. It looks like a healthy run. To exercise a task Action-side, invoke its
116	  worker directly, or move the slot hour in `taskScheduler` and wait for the cron.
117	- **A scheduled task is gated twice — prove a change through `planRun`, never through its own
118	  precondition.** `planRun` computes the due list *before* any precondition runs, so a task whose
119	  most-recent slot has already been run is never evaluated and never reads its signals at all. #513's
120	  forced-run override landed with every test driving the precondition (or the signal collector) directly
121	  and was inert on exactly the run it existed for — the mid-day manual trigger — because the due-list
122	  gate it never touched had already dropped the task (`evaluations: []`; fixed in #516). A test that
123	  starts *inside* the gate proves only "works once evaluated" and says nothing about whether the task
124	  ever gets there. Drive the real `planRun` from a deliberately **non-due** slot: that is the only shape
125	  that catches it.
126	- **Every due task in a run shares ONE checkout — an agentless worker must not touch it.** The
127	  scheduler runs the whole due list in a single working tree, so a worker that checks out a branch or
128	  leaves an index behind hands the next task a tree it did not expect, and a run that dies leaves the
129	  mess for whatever follows. A task whose output is a regenerated file lands it through
130	  `engine/scheduler/deliver-generated.mjs` — git plumbing against the fetched base tip, with HEAD, the
131	  index and the working tree untouched — and reads its prior state from that base rather than local
132	  HEAD, so stacked runs stay idempotent. (`basics/baselining`'s own deliver is the deliberate
133	  exception: it commits a whole working tree under the member's delivery preference.)
134	- **A code-search hit is evidence; a code-search miss is not — survey by reading each file.**
135	- **Derive the test file list from the tree — every hand-written glob here under-runs the suite.**
136	  There is no `package.json` and no test script, so each session invents its own incantation and
137	  silently verifies less than it thinks. Measured in this checkout: `node --test <dir>` does not
138	  recurse — it resolves the path as a module and dies with `Cannot find module`; bash `**` is not
139	  recursive without `globstar`, so `engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs` reaches
140	  **37 of 65** tracked test files. Four consecutive sessions (2026-07-26, #459/#452/#435/#468) each
141	  wrote a different command and reported 587, 690, 621 and 697 tests — three of them pushed after
142	  running a strict subset. Neither published list is authoritative either: `ci.yml`'s `tests=(…)`
143	  array omits `vendoring/*.test.mjs`, and `engine/checks/README.md`'s "as CI runs it" one-liner
144	  names `engine/test/`, `skills/` and `mount/`, none of which exist. So enumerate from git and let
145	  the count speak: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. (The drift-guard, once the array is
146	  clean: assert every tracked `*.test.mjs` is matched by `ci.yml`'s globs.)
147	- **A branch that waited overnight has lost its base *and* possibly its premise — re-verify the
148	  problem still exists on current `main`, unasked.** This repo merges its own scheduled-task PRs
149	  without a human, on top of multi-phase migrations that retire whole directories: measured on
150	  PR #465, `main` moved **14 commits in 13.7 hours** and one of them (#473, "retire `run_daily/`")
151	  *deleted the file the PR's diagnosis rested on* and had already landed most of its content. The
152	  branch rebased cleanly and the tests stayed green — the change was simply no longer the change to
153	  make, and the correct move was `git checkout -B <branch> origin/main` and re-applying only the
154	  surviving slice (9 files → 2). So syncing the base is not the check; the check is a **content**
155	  one: after `git fetch`, read what the new commits did to the surface you are changing and state
156	  whether the problem is still there, what the goal was, and what survives. Do this whenever you
157	  return to a paused branch, before presenting it — the owner should never have to ask "is this
158	  change still needed" (asked three times on #465 before it was volunteered).
159	- **`subscribe_pr_activity` blocks for minutes — subscribe once, and never as a way to "wait for
160	  CI".** It reads like a cheap registration, so a session calls it, gets no answer, and calls it
161	  again on the same PR. Measured in the #520 session (`2026-07-28T2208Z`): two consecutive calls on
162	  PR #524 cost **237s + 220s**, and a `send_later` check-in a further **101s** — **558s of that
163	  session's 841s of total tool wall-clock (66%)**, all pure idle, in a session whose actual work was
164	  153 tool calls. One subscription per PR is all there is to gain; a second adds nothing but the
165	  wait. When what you actually want is "is it green yet", read the check status directly and merge
166	  on the already-green result — don't buy the same notification twice.
167	- **The home has no `.claudinite/shared/` mount — machinery paths must accept both roots.** A
168	  consumer runs the vendored engine under `.claudinite/shared/engine/…` with packs under
169	  `.claudinite/(shared|local)/packs/…`; the home *is* the corpus and runs the same code from the
170	  repo root. So a path, regex, or workflow command written to the consumer mount shape works
171	  fleet-wide and fails on exactly this repo — the last place anyone exercises it, so the break
172	  surfaces late. Write the two-root form up front: make the `.claudinite/(shared|local)/` prefix
173	  optional in a pattern, and in a command probe for `.claudinite/shared/` first, falling back to
174	  the repo root.

# HTML Portable, project-agnostic practices for hand-authored HTML — semantic markup, accessibility, forms, and the document structure pitfalls that recur regardless of framework — true for any HTML read cold. - **Injected block markup inside a `

` silently empties it — read the sibling, not the tag.** When a `

` is filled with raw HTML (e.g. `innerHTML`, or a framework's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html` / `ng-bind-html`), a block element inside it (a `

`, etc.) is disallowed by the HTML content model, so the parser (browser or jsdom, same rule) auto-closes the `

` right before it and the injected content lands as the `

Read `element.nextElementSibling`. - **An ambiguous numeric slash date can't be resolved from its digits — infer the document's convention once, don't guess per-field.** When both parts are ≤ 12 (e.g. `05/07/2026`), resolve the order once per document — never per source or per field — in this order. input.body:
Fulfils the prose-to-checks sweep dispatched in #572 (a task dispatch, so no auto-close).

## What was swept

`packs/` and `.claudinite/local/packs/` — every pack's `RULES.md` and the `SKILL.md`s beside them — read against the check-the-world question from `engine/checks/DESIGN.md`: *does the rule constrain a static signature in the repo artifact?* Dedupe was against the live rule catalog (`packRules`, 65 rules before this change).

Most of what's left in the prose backlog is correctly prose: runtime browser divergence (`web-speech`, `node`'s jsdom rules), in-flight judgment (`spec-driven-product`, `basics`, `research-project`), deployment-time platform behaviour (`aws-sam`), and the `python` pack's own header says its residue is "architecture judgment that has no false-positive-free static signature". One rule stood out as always-testable and unconverted.

## The prose converted

`packs/chrome-extension/RULES.md`:

> A **registered or static content script runs as a *classic* script — it can't be an ES module.** `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts` and static `content_scripts` inject their files as classic scripts (there is no `type: 'module'` mode…), so a top-level `import` in one throws `Uncaught SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module` — **in the host page's console, not the extension's**…

The manifest names the injected files, and a static `import`/`export` in one is a static signature in the source. The failure mode is exactly what a check is for: the script silently never runs, and the SyntaxError lands in a console the extension developer isn't looking at.

## The check: `content-script-module-syntax` (blocking)

`packs/chrome-extension/content-script-module-syntax.mjs`, registered in that pack's `pack.mjs`. Blocking because it is a defect, not a direction — the content script does not run at all.

Parsed, not grepped (the skill's rule — grepping `^import` across an extension would flag the whole codebase, since module syntax is correct everywhere *except* this one injection surface):

- **The judged file set comes from the manifest** — the paths a `content_scripts` entry's `js` array names, resolved against the extension root — plus the `js` string literals on a `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts(...)` call. A module the content script *dynamically* imports is never in that set.
- **Comments stripped and string/template literal contents blanked** before judging, so prose describing the trap and a code string a script builds to inject elsewhere can't fire it.
- **Dynamic `import(...)` — the documented remedy — and `import.meta` are excluded by construction**: the match requires a specifier or a binding right after the keyword, never an opening paren.
- **Self-gates to `[]`** when the repo carries no `manifest.json` declaring `manifest_version`.

The finding's `fix` carries the remedy the prose teaches: register a tiny classic loader whose only statement is `import(chrome.runtime.getURL('…'))`, then list that module and its transitive import graph under `web_accessible_resources`.

## The proving fixture (see-it-fail)

`packs-tests/chrome-extension/content-script-module-syntax.test.mjs` — 7 tests. Neutering `run()` to return `[]` turns all three violating fixtures red and leaves the four guards green, which is the see-it-fail evidence:

| | |
|---|---|
| static `import` in a manifest-declared content script | **red when neutered** (also asserts the imported `lib.js` itself stays quiet) |
| top-level `export default` | **red when neutered** |
| a file declared via `registerContentScripts` | **red when neutered** |
| the classic dynamic-import loader + `import.meta` | quiet (FP guard) |
| module syntax only in a comment / a template literal | quiet (FP guard) |
| the module service worker and a page script | quiet (FP guard) |
| a repo with no extension manifest | quiet (FP guard) |

## Deletion test — the paragraph STAYS

Applied per the skill, and it discriminates rather than deletes here. The finding's `why` carries the rule and the host-page-console diagnostic; its `fix` carries the classic-loader remedy. But the paragraph also carries a **second rule the check does not enforce** — listing the module's *whole transitive import graph* under `web_accessible_resources` gated to the target origins, and having a test walk that graph so a newly added import can't fall out of the list. A paragraph carrying more than the check is not redundant, so it is not trimmed.

## Surface

Bounded to the conversion: the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture test, the pack README's enforcement row, and the corpus tally in `packs/README.md` (65 → 66, which `packs-tests/catalog-tally.test.mjs` guards).

## Green before opening

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` → **1008 pass, 0 fail** (1001 before, +7 new).
- `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` → **exit 0**, 0 blocking, 9 advisory — all pre-existing `file-placement` advisories in `engine/`, none touched by this change.

## What was swept

`packs/` and `.claudinite/local/packs/` — every pack's `RULES.md` and the `SKILL.md`s beside them — read against the check-the-world question from `engine/checks/DESIGN.md`: *does the rule constrain a static signature in the repo artifact?* Dedupe was against the live rule catalog (`packRules`, 65 rules before this change).

Most of what's left in the prose backlog is correctly prose: runtime browser divergence (`web-speech`, `node`'s jsdom rules), in-flight judgment (`spec-driven-product`, `basics`, `research-project`), deployment-time platform behaviour (`aws-sam`), and the `python` pack's own header says its residue is "architecture judgment that has no false-positive-free static signature". One rule stood out as always-testable and unconverted.

## The prose converted

`packs/chrome-extension/RULES.md`:

> A **registered or static content script runs as a *classic* script — it can't be an ES module.** `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts` and static `content_scripts` inject their files as classic scripts (there is no `type: 'module'` mode…), so a top-level `import` in one throws `Uncaught SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module` — **in the host page's console, not the extension's**…

The manifest names the injected files, and a static `import`/`export` in one is a static signature in the source. The failure mode is exactly what a check is for: the script silently never runs, and the SyntaxError lands in a console the extension developer isn't looking at.

## The check: `content-script-module-syntax` (blocking)

`packs/chrome-extension/content-script-module-syntax.mjs`, registered in that pack's `pack.mjs`. Blocking because it is a defect, not a direction — the content script does not run at all.

Parsed, not grepped (the skill's rule — grepping `^import` across an extension would flag the whole codebase, since module syntax is correct everywhere *except* this one injection surface):

- **The judged file set comes from the manifest** — the paths a `content_scripts` entry's `js` array names, resolved against the extension root — plus the `js` string literals on a `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts(...)` call. A module the content script *dynamically* imports is never in that set.
- **Comments stripped and string/template literal contents blanked** before judging, so prose describing the trap and a code string a script builds to inject elsewhere can't fire it.
- **Dynamic `import(...)` — the documented remedy — and `import.meta` are excluded by construction**: the match requires a specifier or a binding right after the keyword, never an opening paren.
- **Self-gates to `[]`** when the repo carries no `manifest.json` declaring `manifest_version`.

The finding's `fix` carries the remedy the prose teaches: register a tiny classic loader whose only statement is `import(chrome.runtime.getURL('…'))`, then list that module and its transitive import graph under `web_accessible_resources`.

| | |
|---|---|
| static `import` in a manifest-declared content script | **red when neutered** (also asserts the imported `lib.js` itself stays quiet) |
| top-level `export default` | **red when neutered** |
| a file declared via `registerContentScripts` | **red when neutered** |
| the classic dynamic-import loader + `import.meta` | quiet (FP guard) |
| module syntax only in a comment / a template literal | quiet (FP guard) |
| the module service worker and a page script | quiet (FP guard) |
| a repo with no extension manifest | quiet (FP guard) |

## Deletion test — the paragraph STAYS

Applied per the skill, and it discriminates rather than deletes here. The finding's `why` carries the rule and the host-page-console diagnostic; its `fix` carries the classic-loader remedy. But the paragraph also carries a **second rule the check does not enforce** — listing the module's *whole transitive import graph* under `web_accessible_resources` gated to the target origins, and having a test walk that graph so a newly added import can't fall out of the list. A paragraph carrying more than the check is not redundant, so it is not trimmed.

Bounded to the conversion: the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture test, the pack README's enforcement row, and the corpus tally in `packs/README.md` (65 → 66, which `packs-tests/catalog-tally.test.mjs` guards).
